medium.titulo: Engineering a Production AI Assistant: Securing a Paid LLM Endpoint (Part 2/3)
medium.conteudo_html:
By Jawher Ennaceur :Linkedin

This is the second part of a series on building and shipping the AI assistant that lives on my portfolio. Part 1, “Keeping Answers True to Your Data”, covered the assistant’s knowledge layer and its behavior. Part 3, “Tests, Launch and Real Numbers”, covers how I verified the whole system in layers, what the launch checklist looked like, and what the first weeks in production showed.

Summary

1 — Introduction: A Portfolio That Answers Back
2 — The Problem: What Could Go Wrong With a Paid Public Route
3 — The Core Idea: Free Checks First, Closed on Doubt
4 — Proving You’re Human Once: Turnstile and a Signed Cookie
5 — Counting in the Right Place: Why Serverless Needs Redis
6 — From Message Counts to Dollars
7 — Watching It, and What I Choose Not to Log
8 — A Worked Example
9 — Trade-offs and Limits
10 — Conclusion: Bounded, but Unproven

1. Introduction: The Same curl, Again

Previously, in Part 1: I built the knowledge layer of the assistant: typed items, a compact index, bounded tools and a behavior contract that keeps the model from inventing facts. That left a route that anyone can call and that bills me for every message.
Part 1 ended with this request, and I’m going to send it again:

curl -X POST https://my-portfolio.example/api/chat \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'

Against a bare version of the route, that command just works. It works the hundredth time and the ten-thousandth, from any machine, with no account and no cookie, and every answer is billed to me by the token. By my estimates a typical answer costs a cent or two, which sounds harmless until you picture a script sending it in a loop while I sleep. My own first version had a small counter in memory, and why that wasn’t enough is the story of section 5.

This article is about closing that gap. The setup is the one from Part 1, a Next.js route on Vercel in front of a Gemini model, with Upstash Redis for the counters and Cloudflare Turnstile for the human check. I start with what someone could realistically do to a route like this, then walk through the checks in the order they run, and end with the part I care about most: turning “don’t let it cost too much” into a number in dollars that the code enforces before every call.

The quality of the answers was Part 1’s subject, and numbers from real traffic belong to Part 3, so what I can show here is the mechanisms and the tests that prove them, with every estimate labeled as one. At the end, I’ll send the same command again and show what it gets back.

2. The Problem: What Could Go Wrong With a Paid Public Route

I can’t put the assistant behind a login. Someone skimming my portfolio has little patience for an account form, and it would end the visit before the first question. So the route stays open to strangers, and the strangers I worry about don’t behave like visitors.

I came up with five, and I’m keeping only the threats I have an answer for, since a list of fears without a fix is decoration.

Two of these need a comment. The assistant refuses off-topic requests, as Part 1 showed, but a refusal still costs a model call, so good behavior is not free. And the last row isn’t hypothetical: while testing on the free tier, which allows about 20 requests a day for this model, I used them all myself. Nothing in my code was wrong, and the assistant answered with an error (it now tells visitors it is very busy). A quota someone else sets can run out whether or not anyone attacks you.

From these I wrote three goals I can check, not just hope for. First, the worst case for one message has a number I can compute. Second, a rejected request costs as little as possible: free checks first, then those that need Redis, and only a request that passes everything reaches the model. Third, when in doubt the route says no: if Redis is down or a secret is missing in production, the chat refuses to run instead of running unprotected.

The third is the easiest to verify, because the tests exist:

PASS  rate-limit store down -> fails closed (503)
PASS  production without Redis/Turnstile/secret -> 503

The first two take the next sections to explain, and the second has an exception I’ll own up to in section 3.

3. The Core Idea: Free Checks First, Closed on Doubt

Every check in front of the model exists to refuse a request, so the useful question is what a refusal costs me. My rule is that nothing that spends money runs before something that is free. In practice that gives four tiers: checks that only read the environment or headers, one that does a little cryptography, two that call Redis, and the model, which is the only step that bills me by the token. The guard runs them in that order, and a request stops at the first one it fails:

// lib/assistant/guard.ts, abridged
const base = baseChecks(request);          // kill switch, config, origin
if (base) return fail(base);
if (declaredBodySize > maxBodyBytes) return fail(413);     // header only, no body read
if (!verifySessionToken(cookie, secret)) return fail(401); // HMAC check, no network
const budget = await checkBudget(store, ip);               // 3 Redis reads
if (!budget.ok) return fail(429);
const limit = await checkMessageLimits(store, ip);         // up to 4 Redis increments
if (!limit.ok) return fail(429);

Notice that Redis comes after the cookie. A visitor with no valid cookie, which includes anyone with a script, never causes a Redis call on this route. Within Redis, I read budgets before I write rate-limit counters, because reading is cheaper than incrementing and a visitor refused on budget shouldn’t move any counter.

The exception

One check breaks the rule. Validating the body is free, yet it runs after both Redis steps, in the route, because the guard is one function that runs first and parsing happens after it. It has a side effect I can live with: malformed requests count against the rate limit, so flooding the route with garbage gets throttled too. If I validated earlier, garbage would stop costing Redis calls but would also stop counting. I haven’t changed it. A header can also lie about the body size, which I come back to in section 9.

The origin check is weaker than it looks

It compares the Origin header with the host, but only when the header is present, and a curl command doesn't send one. What it stops is JavaScript on another website using a visitor's browser to call my route. A script on its own machine passes straight through it, and the check that stops that script is the session cookie. That is why the curl from the introduction fails at the cookie, not at the origin.

Closed on doubt

The other half of the rule is what happens when I’m unsure. In production the route refuses to run unless everything it depends on is configured:

export function productionProblems(): string[] {
  if (!isProd()) return [];
  const problems: string[] = [];
  if (!redisConfig()) problems.push("Redis (...)");
  if (!turnstileSecret()) problems.push("TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY");
  if (!sessionSecret()) problems.push("CHAT_SESSION_SECRET (at least 32 characters)");
  return problems;
}

If that list isn’t empty, both chat endpoints return 503 and the log names the missing variable. The same attitude covers failures at runtime: if Redis throws while I’m counting, the request gets a 503, never a pass. In development, none of this applies. Counters live in memory, the session secret has a built-in default and the Turnstile check is skipped when no key is set, so I can work without any account. Production has no such fallbacks. The price is availability: if I forget a variable at deploy, the assistant is down. I would rather find that out myself than discover later that it ran without limits.

That leaves the cookie, the one check that actually stops a script. Where it comes from is the next section.

4. Proving You’re Human Once: Turnstile and a Signed Cookie

The human check is Cloudflare Turnstile, a free challenge that usually runs invisibly in the visitor’s browser and produces a token. I could verify one of those with every message, and I decided not to, for three reasons. A token can be validated only once and expires after 300 seconds, according to Cloudflare’s documentation, so every message would need a fresh challenge. Each verification is also a round trip to Cloudflare in the middle of a conversation. And a challenge that sometimes asks for interaction is a poor thing to repeat on every question.

So the token is spent once, on a separate endpoint, and exchanged for a cookie that my own server can check without calling anyone. The cookie has three parts, joined by dots:

payload = "<expiry, unix seconds>.<8 random bytes>"
token   = payload + "." + HMAC-SHA256(payload, CHAT_SESSION_SECRET)
Set-Cookie: chat_session=<token>; Path=/api/chat; Max-Age=1800;
            HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Secure

It lasts 30 minutes. HttpOnly keeps page scripts from reading it, SameSite=Strict stops other sites from sending it, and the path means it only travels to the chat endpoints. Secure is on in production only, because my local server runs on plain http.

Checking the cookie on each message needs no database and no Redis, which is why it sits before them in the guard:

// abridged from lib/assistant/session.ts
const parts = token.split(".");
if (parts.length !== 3) return false;
const payload = `${parts[0]}.${parts[1]}`;
const expected = Buffer.from(sign(payload, secret));
const given = Buffer.from(parts[2]);
if (expected.length !== given.length || !timingSafeEqual(expected, given)) return false;
return Number(parts[0]) * 1000 > now;   // not expired

I recompute the signature and compare it with timingSafeEqual, which takes the same time wherever the two values differ, so nobody can guess a signature one character at a time by timing the responses. Two tests cover the failure paths, one that changes the last character of a valid token and one that checks it after its expiry:

PASS  tampered session token fails
PASS  expired session token fails

The session endpoint has its own guard. It allows 10 attempts per minute per visitor, so my route can’t be used to hammer Cloudflare, and it fails closed: any error, a timeout (5 seconds) or an answer other than success from Cloudflare means no cookie. When a cookie expires mid-conversation, the next message gets a 401, and the chat window runs the check once more and retries.

The trade-off is real. Some guides warn that turning a verified token into a session flag reopens the replay window, and that is what this design does. The cookie proves a challenge was passed within the last 30 minutes, not that a human is sending this message, and someone who solves one challenge can reuse it until it expires. I accept that because the cookie only unlocks an endpoint that is already limited per visitor and capped in dollars, which is what the next two sections are about.

5. Counting in the Right Place: Why Serverless Needs Redis

My first version of the rate limiter was a Map in memory: for each IP address, a list of recent timestamps, and a refusal after six messages in a minute. It passed its tests and it would have been nearly useless on Vercel. The route doesn't run on one server. It runs as short-lived functions, spread over however many instances the traffic needs, and each instance has its own memory and starts with an empty counter. A visitor's requests can land on three different instances, and none of them sees more than a third of the traffic.

The fix is to move the counters out of the instances and into one place they all share, which for me is Upstash Redis. The counters are fixed windows: the window is part of the key, so a new minute is simply a new key and nothing ever needs to be reset.

chat:ip:{visitor}:m:{minute}   expires after 2 minutes    one visitor, one minute
chat:ip:{visitor}:d:{day}      expires after 25 hours      one visitor, one day
chat:g:d:{day}                 expires after 25 hours      everyone, one day
chat:g:M:{month}               expires after 32 days       everyone, one month

{minute} is the current time divided by 60,000 milliseconds and rounded down, so every request in the same minute increments the same key. Writing is two Redis calls:

const n = await redis.incrby(key, amount);
if (n === amount) await redis.expire(key, ttlSeconds);  // the key was just created

Those two calls aren’t atomic, and they don’t need to be. If the function dies between them, the key stays without an expiry, but its name contains the window, so nothing reads it after the window ends. The cost is a stray key, which I come back to in section 9, along with the main weakness of fixed windows.

The visitor in those keys is a hash of the IP address, not the address itself. What that does and doesn’t protect is a question for section 7. What matters here is the order: a message is counted against the visitor’s minute, then the visitor’s day, then the global day, then the global month, and the first limit exceeded ends the check. A visitor who is already blocked therefore never touches the shared counters, so one abuser can’t use more than their own share of the budget. A test with a fake clock checks the first of those limits:

PASS  per-minute limit blocks after 6
PASS  another visitor is unaffected

I didn’t compare this with the rate-limiting libraries or the platform’s own firewall rules, so I can’t claim mine is better. One thing I’m glad of is that the same small store, three methods behind one interface, later carried the dollar counters in the next section too.

6. From Message Counts to Dollars

A message cap counts requests, and requests are not what I pay in. Two messages can cost me about one cent or about fourteen, so “3,000 messages a month” can mean about $30 or about $400, depending on what those messages look like. That is why the first goal in section 2 was a number for the worst case of a single message, and why that number has to come before any budget.

Bounding one message

Every limit that matters is already in the code. A message makes at most five model calls, each capped at 1,500 output tokens, thinking tokens included. The newest message can be 8,000 characters, and the history sent to the model is the last eight messages, with older ones cut to 1,200 characters. From that I can compute a ceiling, rounding up where I’m unsure:

system prompt + index   about 2,560 tokens (measured, characters / 4)
history                 up to 4,100 tokens (8,000 + 7 x 1,200 characters)
one tool result         up to 2,000 tokens (my rounded-up ceiling)
input  = 5 x (2,560 + 4,100) + 2,000 x (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4)   about 53,000 tokens
output = 5 x 1,500                                             7,500 tokens

Every call resends the whole context, and each later call also carries the tool results of the earlier ones, which is why the input is so much larger than the output.

Turning tokens into dollars

I store money as integers in micro-dollars, so Redis only needs the same INCRBY as the rate limits. A price quoted per million tokens is, conveniently, the same number as micro-dollars per token, so the cost is one multiplication:

export const costMicro = (inputTokens: number, outputTokens: number, prices = getPrices()) =>
  Math.ceil(inputTokens * prices.inputPerM + outputTokens * prices.outputPerM);

Output includes thinking tokens, which the provider bills as output, so the code counts the larger of the reported output and text plus reasoning. When the provider reports no usage at all, I estimate from the text, about four characters per token, so the cap doesn’t silently count zero. Before each call, the budget stage from section 3 reads three totals: everyone today, everyone this month, and this visitor today. The defaults are small on purpose: $1 a day and $10 a month for everyone, and $0.30 a day per visitor, so one visitor can’t spend more than 30 cents of the shared budget.

What it guarantees, and what it doesn’t

Prices first, because they change. As of October 2026, Gemini 3.6 Flash is listed at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, with a rise to $1.50 and $7.50 announced from January 1, 2027, and older sources still show the higher figures (see the sources at the end). Recheck before relying on any of this.

That table is why the message cap alone isn’t enough: 3,000 typical messages cost $31 to $63, while 3,000 maximal ones would cost $204 to $409. The dollar budgets change the picture. At the higher prices, $0.30 a day covers about three maximal messages for one visitor, because the check runs before the call and the message that crosses the line still completes. A shared $10 a month covers about 73 maximal messages, or roughly 480 typical ones. Two tests cover the budget checks:

PASS  per-visitor dollar budget blocks that visitor
PASS  monthly dollar budget blocks everyone

Two gaps remain. Because the check happens before the call and the cost is recorded after it, several messages in flight can all pass together. The overshoot is at most the number in flight times the cost of a maximal message, and I expect a few cents, though I haven’t measured it. Cost is also recorded only for model calls that finish. If a visitor closes the tab mid-call, or a call hits the 45 second timeout, those tokens are never counted, so the counters undercount exactly when something goes wrong. The message caps limit how often that can happen.

The provider can also say no first. When it answers 429, the chat tells the visitor that the assistant is busy instead of showing a generic error, and my own budgets are only useful if they sit well under the provider’s quota, so that mine are the ones that trigger.

All of this is code I wrote, so a bug of mine could bypass every line of it. The second cap has to live outside my code: a budget and alerts on the provider’s side, a quota on the API if the console offers one, and a separate production key and project. As far as I know, budget alerts notify rather than stop spending, and I haven’t verified what Google’s console can enforce, so I treat that as a warning system and my own budgets as the brake. I set it up in Part 3.

7. Watching It, and What I Choose Not to Log

Two questions decide whether I trust this system after launch: how much has it cost so far, and is anything going wrong. The counters from the last section hold the answers, but nobody can read a Redis counter at a glance, so every message also leaves a trace somewhere I can look.

One line per message

When a message finishes, the route writes one structured line to the host’s logs, with no message text in it. This is its shape, with invented values:

{"evt":"chat_usage","visitor":"a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8","ok":true,"steps":2,
 "tools":["get_item"],"inputTokens":8421,"outputTokens":930,
 "reasoningTokens":310,"costUsd":0.0196,"ms":4210}

It tells me how many model calls the message took, which tools ran, what it cost by my estimate and how long it took. Two fields appear only when they matter: an estimated flag when the provider reported no tokens, which is how I'll notice the fallback from section 6, and an errorCode on failures, where a 429 from the provider would show up.

A report I can call

Logs are good for single messages and poor for totals, so a private endpoint sums the counters:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHAT_ADMIN_TOKEN" https://my-portfolio.example/api/chat/usage
{ "day": { "messages": 41, "costUsd": 0.52, "budgetUsd": 1, "usedPercent": 52 }, "month": { "...": "..." } }

The response above is trimmed and its values are invented. The endpoint answers 404 unless a token of at least 24 characters is configured, so a deployment without one doesn’t announce that the route exists. A wrong token gets a 401, compared in constant time like the cookie, and guesses are throttled to 10 a minute per visitor:

PASS  usage endpoint rejects a wrong token (401)

Alerts

I don’t want to find out by looking. After each message, the route compares the day’s and the month’s spending with their budgets and emails me at 80 percent and again at 100 percent, once each: the first message to cross a level claims a Redis counter, and later ones find it already taken. It reuses the contact form’s email service, and stays silent if that isn’t configured.

What I choose not to log

My code never writes message text to the logs or to Redis. Visitors may paste a job description or something personal, and I’d rather not hold it. The conversation itself stays in the visitor’s own browser tab. The model provider does receive every message, which no choice of mine can undo, and the chat window says so.

Raw IP addresses aren’t stored either, but I should be precise about what the replacement buys. Counters and log lines carry a hash of the address, a plain SHA-256 cut to 16 characters, and IPv4 has only about four billion addresses, so anyone holding the logs can hash a candidate and check whether it appears. That makes it a pseudonym, not anonymity, and under rules like the GDPR a pseudonymous identifier is still personal data. These identifiers live in Redis for up to three days, and in the logs for as long as my host keeps them.

The price of that choice

I can’t read a wrong answer after the fact. I can see that a message took three calls and cost two cents, but not what it said. How I plan to compensate belongs to Part 3. For now, I can finally watch the thing I started with, and the next section sends that same command again.

8. A Worked Example: The Same curl, Now Refused

Here is the command from the introduction, sent to a route that has all the checks from this article. I ran the real guard code in production mode, with fake configuration and in-memory counters, so what follows is the code’s behavior, not traffic from my live site:

curl -X POST https://my-portfolio.example/api/chat \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
HTTP 401
{"error":"Please complete the security check."}

It gets past the origin check, because curl sends no Origin header, and it stops at the session cookie, before any Redis call or model call. It costs me nothing, and it leaves only a status code in my host's request log. Three more cases show the remaining layers:

The script in the first row holds a valid cookie, so it passes the human check, and what stops it is the rate limit from section 5. That is the replayed cookie from section 4 meeting its second line of defense. The second row is the overshoot from section 6 in miniature. Each maximal message costs about 13.6 cents at the higher prices. The third one passed the check with 27 cents spent against a 30 cent budget, finished, and left the visitor at about 41 cents, so the fourth was refused. I spent roughly 11 cents more than the budget, and the next visitor was unaffected.

The Redis row is the price of failing closed: everyone gets a 503, honest visitors included, until the store is back. The last row matters most to me. A normal visitor sends one message, passes every check and notices nothing, though I haven’t measured how much latency the extra Redis calls add. That belongs to Part 3.

One gap shows in the last column. My code writes a usage line only when a message reaches the model, so refusals appear in my host’s request log as status codes and nowhere else. A burst of 401s or 429s would be visible there, but I haven’t built a counter for refusals of my own.

9. Trade-offs and Limits

Everything in this article bets that some failures are acceptable if they are bounded and visible. These are the ones I know about that haven’t come up yet, with what would make me change each. The replayed cookie, the overshoot and the uncounted calls were covered where they arose, so I won’t repeat them.

Counting

Fixed windows are blunt. A visitor can send six messages at the end of one minute and six more at the start of the next, twelve in a couple of seconds, with every counter satisfied. A sliding window would close that at the cost of more Redis calls per message, and at six a minute I haven’t found it worth it.

“Per visitor” really means “per IP address”. Several people behind one office or university network share one budget, and the message they get says to come back tomorrow, a poor first impression for a recruiter. Someone with many addresses gets a budget for each, which the global caps contain rather than prevent. The header I read is x-forwarded-for, and on Vercel it is the visitor's address. But Vercel's documentation says that when a proxy sits in front, they overwrite the header and do not forward external IPs, so every visitor would look like one address and share one limit. I'd learn that from the first complaints, not from an alarm.

A key can also outlive its window. INCRBY and EXPIRE aren't atomic, so a function that dies between them leaves a counter with no expiry. Nothing reads it, so the cost is a stray key, and a cleanup job would remove any that pile up.

Trusting what the visitor sends

The size check reads the Content-Length header, which a client can omit or misreport. The character limits apply after parsing, so a hostile body is read before it is refused. I assume the platform's own request size limit is the backstop and haven't checked what it is. Turnstile verification also ignores two fields in Cloudflare's response, hostname and action. The site key is used only by this route and the widget only works on my domains, so I judged the risk small, but the checks would take a few lines and I haven't written them.

The budget that protects my wallet can also be used against everyone else. Whoever empties the day’s budget switches the assistant off for every visitor until tomorrow. That trades availability for cost, and the code sides with cost. If it happens, the answer is to raise the cap with eyes open, not to remove it.

Depending on others

Two external services now sit on the critical path. When Redis is down the assistant is off, by design, and Turnstile means a script from another company loads in the visitor’s browser. I accept both, but they are real dependencies for a feature that used to need only my code and a model API. The fastest emergency stop isn’t CHAT_ENABLED, since changing a variable needs a redeploy. It is revoking the provider's key, which cuts off the source of the spending, and I'd rather know that before the day I need it. Finally, the detector that watches for the system prompt in answers is a safety net, not a guarantee. It gets its own explanation in Part 3.

10. Conclusion: Bounded, but Unproven

The mistake I nearly made was treating a message cap as a cost cap. Two messages can differ in price by a factor of fourteen, so the number that holds is a dollar figure, computed from the limits in my own code and checked before every call. Around it sit cheap refusals in front of the expensive step, and a habit of saying no when something I depend on is missing. None of it is clever, but each piece closes a hole I can point to: a script that never touched the site, counters that lived in the wrong memory, a bill nobody had added up.

The command that opened this article now stops at the cookie, costs me nothing and leaves a status code in my host’s log. I can also say how much a single message can cost me at most, which I couldn’t have said when I started.

What I can’t say yet is whether any of this survives real visitors. Everything here ran against a fake clock, a fake Redis and a pretend Cloudflare, with prices I looked up and token counts I estimated. My “cent or two” per message is a guess until a bill agrees with it, and the cost of failing closed, an assistant that is off when it shouldn’t be, only shows up in use.

That is Part 3, “Engineering a Production AI Assistant: Tests, Launch and Real Numbers”. It covers how I tested all of this in layers, from fake services to the real model, what the launch checklist looked like, the prompt-leak detector I left out here, and what the first weeks in production said about the estimates I made in this article.

TL;DR

AI may not be reducing the need for workers as much as it is exposing how modern work is organized. While it automates many repetitive tasks, it also creates new responsibilities around guiding, reviewing, and validating its output. The result is often not less work, but different work. More importantly, AI is revealing something that existed long before AI itself: many organizations are still built around filling a fixed number of working hours rather than maximizing value creation. As routine work disappears, companies will increasingly have to distinguish between work that is genuinely necessary and work that merely keeps people busy.

The real impact of AI may not be job replacement. It may be the end of artificial work.

—

For years, the debate around artificial intelligence has revolved around a single question: will AI replace jobs? The answers usually fall somewhere between “almost all of them” and “hardly any.” Both sides often make the same mistake. They treat work as a fixed amount of tasks that are currently done by humans and could eventually be done by machines.

That is not how work operates inside most organizations.

A common argument today is the decline of junior hiring. Many point to this as evidence that AI is already replacing entry-level workers. The conclusion is less obvious than it seems. Junior roles have traditionally been the first positions to disappear during economic downturns. When companies face uncertainty, they reduce training costs, slow hiring, and rely more heavily on experienced employees. This pattern existed long before AI.

AI may be contributing to the decline of junior positions, but the current labor market matters as well. Many organizations are hiring more cautiously across the board. Looking at fewer junior openings and attributing the entire trend to AI is likely an oversimplification.

Another common assumption is that if workers become more productive with AI, companies will simply need fewer of them. If five people can suddenly do the work of ten, then surely only three or four employees will be necessary.

It sounds reasonable.

History suggests otherwise.

Major productivity gains have rarely led to a proportional reduction in work. More often, organizations increase output, expand their scope, enter new markets, or take on projects that were previously not feasible. The additional capacity gets absorbed.

Something similar is already happening with AI.

The work itself is not disappearing. It is changing.

Anyone who uses AI regularly knows that the idea of pressing a button and receiving a finished result has little connection to reality. AI generates drafts, analyses, code, recommendations, and documentation. It also creates misunderstandings, inconsistencies, false assumptions, and errors. A significant part of the job becomes keeping the system on track.

One task turns into several.

You need to define the problem correctly. You need to evaluate the output. You need to detect mistakes. You need to validate results. You need to refine prompts, provide context, correct assumptions, and review everything again.

In environments where quality matters, human work does not disappear. It shifts from execution to supervision, judgment, and validation.

What is often overlooked is that many of the tasks being removed by AI served a purpose beyond their immediate output. Routine work helped structure the day. Between complex tasks, there were periods of lower cognitive demand. People could process emails, update documents, prepare presentations, organize data, or perform other repetitive activities. These tasks were rarely the most valuable part of the job, but they created mental breathing room.

As AI removes more of this work, a larger share of the day becomes focused on decisions, evaluation, and problem solving. The workload does not necessarily decrease. In many cases, it becomes more cognitively demanding. This is already visible across many knowledge-based professions. People often produce more than before, yet do not feel less busy.

There is another point that receives surprisingly little attention.

Long before AI, many organizations contained a significant amount of work with limited value. That is not necessarily the result of poor management. It is often a consequence of how modern work is structured. Most companies still operate around a model inherited from an industrial era: eight hours a day, five days a week. That model made sense when output was closely tied to time. The longer someone worked on an assembly line, the more products were produced.

Knowledge work functions differently.

Most office workers experience quiet periods where little happens, followed by intense periods that require overtime. Workloads fluctuate naturally. Yet organizations are often designed around the assumption of constant utilization.

The result is predictable. During slower periods, people find ways to fill time. Meetings are added. Reports are expanded. Processes become more complicated. Work emerges because workers are available, not always because the work is necessary.

In this environment, AI may not be replacing large amounts of valuable work. It may be removing activities that existed primarily because time needed to be filled. That does not automatically translate into unemployment. Instead, it exposes a reality that many organizations have avoided confronting. Once low-value tasks disappear, companies are forced to think more carefully about what outcomes actually matter. The question is no longer how to keep someone occupied for eight hours. It becomes how much value that person creates.

This may be where the long-term impact of AI truly lies.

Not in the wholesale replacement of workers, but in revealing problems that already existed. For decades, organizations optimized around time. AI may force them to optimize around value instead.

That does not mean nobody will lose their job. Some tasks will disappear. Some professions will shrink. Others will emerge. Every major technological shift has produced winners, losers, and entirely new categories of work.

The larger change may happen elsewhere.

If AI takes over a substantial share of administrative and repetitive work, then the real question becomes whether the current structure of knowledge work still makes sense. The future may involve shorter workweeks, different employment models, or new ways of organizing expertise and responsibility.

The most important story about AI may not be that humans are being replaced by machines.

It may be that AI is revealing how much of modern work was already misaligned with the kind of work people actually do.

medium.titulo: AI effort levels: Choosing low, medium, high or max in LLM’s
medium.resumo: Every major AI model now lets you choose how much thinking happens before an answer. OpenAI and xAI call the setting reasoning effort…
medium.conteudo_html:
Every major AI model now lets you choose how much thinking happens before an answer. OpenAI and xAI call the setting reasoning effort, Anthropic calls it effort, and Qwen pairs thinking mode with effort levels. In the apps, you will find Instant through Extra High in ChatGPT, an Effort menu in Claude, and Fast, Expert and Heavy in Grok.

That choice affects answer quality, waiting time and cost. This guide covers the vendors’ implementations as of October 2026, the measured differences between levels and the tasks each level suits.

In short:

  • Effort controls the tokens spent on reasoning, tool calls and the answer. Reasoning tokens count as billable output even when they remain invisible.
  • Gains diminish quickly. GPT-6.1 Sol gains six points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index from low to medium. The next three steps add four points combined, while max costs about five and a half times as much per task as low.
  • Medium is a useful starting point for most work. Choose low or off for simple tasks at volume, and reserve xhigh or max for long agentic runs where your evaluations demonstrate a gain.

What AI effort levels control

An effort level tells a reasoning model how much work to devote to its response. Before answering, the model generates internal reasoning tokens to break down the problem, explore approaches and check its work. Effort influences how many tokens it uses.

This is test-time compute: giving the same model more computation per question instead of choosing a larger model. OpenAI’s reasoning guide describes the trade-off between faster, leaner responses at lower effort and more complete thinking at higher effort. The setting guides the model rather than imposing a hard cap. A difficult problem can still prompt reasoning at low effort, just less than at high.

What changes when you increase effort?

Quality, waiting time and price all change, but not in proportion.

Quality improves, then the gains flatten

Hard tasks benefit from more effort, though each step brings a smaller return. Artificial Analysis benchmarks the same model at each setting, isolating effort’s effect. Its GPT-6.1 Sol results illustrate the pattern.

These figures were read on 8 October 2026. The index combines ten evaluations, from agentic coding to long-context reasoning. Low to medium buys six points for eight additional cents per task. Medium to max adds four points while more than tripling the cost. The final step alone almost doubles spending for one point.

Speed: more tokens, rather than slower typing

Higher effort takes longer because the model generates more tokens. Its generation speed does not necessarily fall. Artificial Analysis reports GPT-6.1 Sol output speeds of 49 to 56 tokens per second across all five settings. QwenCloud documentation provides another perspective: reasoning accounted for over 60 percent of qwen3.7-plus output tokens, and disabling thinking reduced total latency by 60 to 75 percent.

Cost: invisible thinking still appears on the bill

Reasoning tokens are billed as output, at three to five times the input rate for the models covered here. Our guide to tokens in AI explains token pricing.

Consider a request with 3,000 input tokens and a 500-token answer, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Those are the list rates for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol. The reasoning counts below are illustrative: OpenAI says one request can consume anything from a few hundred to tens of thousands of reasoning tokens.

The token rate stays constant, but the bill increases almost fifteenfold. Benchmarks show the effect at scale. Artificial Analysis measured Claude Sonnet 5.5 consuming about 193,000 output tokens per task at max, roughly seven times GPT-6 Astra’s consumption at its own max setting.

Effort levels in ChatGPT and the OpenAI API

ChatGPT exposes thinking levels in its model picker. The API uses reasoning.effort.

Thinking levels in ChatGPT

Since the October 2026 GPT-6 rollout began, the Thinking slider offers Instant, Medium, High, Extra High and Pro. OpenAI’s help centre identifies GPT-6 Sol as the model behind the first four. Pro uses GPT-6 Pro, powered by GPT-6 Astra.

Plus includes Instant, Medium and High. Extra High and Pro require Pro, Business or Enterprise. Free and Go users have one Think option, running on GPT-5.6 Luna.

On Plus and Pro, Instant no longer automatically increases the level for complex questions. You need to select it yourself.

Reasoning effort in the API

The Responses API accepts none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max for reasoning.effort, with a different supported subset for each model. GPT-6 Astra excludes none. GPT-6.1 Sol excludes both none and minimal, defaulting to medium. A separate pro mode allows GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 models to work harder on difficult tasks independently of effort.

OpenAI’s listed prices per million input/output tokens are $10/$50 for GPT-6 Astra, $2/$10 for GPT-6.1 Sol and $0.10/$0.50 for GPT-6 Luna.

Effort levels in Claude

Claude’s newest models offer low, medium, high, xhigh and max.

Effort in the apps

The effort control sits in the model menu beside the send button. Each model’s recommended setting is labelled Default. Anthropic’s help centre advises using defaults for everyday work and Max for the hardest tasks where correctness is critical. Higher effort takes longer and consumes plan limits faster.

Effort in the API

The API parameter is output_config.effort. Anthropic’s documentation says most Claude models default to high, while Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium. Omitting effort therefore runs Opus 5.5 one level below Opus 5. Anthropic recommends low for fast, inexpensive work such as subagents, and xhigh for agentic and coding tasks lasting more than 30 minutes.

Effort covers all output tokens, including tool calls. At low effort, agents make fewer and shorter tool calls. Adaptive thinking is always enabled on Claude Opus 5.5, making effort the main control for reasoning depth and cost.

Anthropic’s prices per million input/output tokens are $4/$20 for Opus 5.5, $2/$10 for Sonnet 5.5 and $0.10/$0.50 for Haiku 5.5 on prompts up to 100,000 tokens.

Effort levels in Qwen

Qwen provides the most granular controls of these four vendors: a thinking switch, a token budget and named levels. Many models can also run on your own hardware.

QwenCloud documentation says hybrid models use enable_thinking to switch reasoning on or off per request. Thinking-only models always reason. The thinking_budget parameter limits thinking tokens; once exhausted, the model answers immediately. Newer models add reasoning_effort, with low, medium and xhigh available on qwen3.8-max.

That model defaults to xhigh, its most expensive setting, and rejects requests combining reasoning_effort with thinking_budget. For open-source Qwen3 hybrid models, adding /no_think to a message skips reasoning for that turn.

QwenCloud lists qwen3.8-max at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. Some hybrid models have different rates in thinking mode. With open-weight models such as Qwen3.8–27B, also defaulting to xhigh, effort consumes GPU time and adds latency instead of generating a per-token charge. It therefore affects hardware sizing.

Effort levels in Grok

Current Grok models always reason. You control the amount of thinking, but cannot disable it.

xAI’s reasoning documentation lists low, medium, high and xhigh for grok-4.7 and grok-4.6, defaulting to high. Grok-4.5 goes only as far as high. For grok-4.20-multi-agent, the same parameter chooses four or sixteen agents instead of changing one model’s reasoning time. Grok 4.7 costs $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

In the apps, Fast prioritises speed, Expert thinks harder and Auto selects between them. Heavy assigns a team of agents for SuperGrok Heavy subscribers. See our complete guide to Grok AI for more on the product.

Comparing ChatGPT, Claude, Qwen and Grok

Each vendor provides a fast option, a balanced default and one or two settings for the hardest tasks.

Choosing an effort level for the task

Start with the work rather than the model. The right setting depends on the reasoning required and the consequences of an incorrect answer. This table brings together the vendors’ recommendations.

For high-volume work, begin one level below your initial estimate and test whether quality holds. Savings accumulate across requests. When an error is expensive, such as an incorrect figure in a board report, start one level higher and still verify the answer.

Is more effort always better?

No. Additional thinking helps when reasoning is necessary, but can hurt other tasks. Researchers working with Anthropic designed tasks where longer reasoning reduced accuracy. Models became distracted by irrelevant details, followed misleading patterns or lost track of constraints.

Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 guidance says max adds substantial cost for small gains on most workloads and can lead to overthinking on structured-output tasks. Effort cannot compensate for an unclear prompt. OpenAI’s reasoning guide therefore prioritises a clear goal, constraints and output format.

Increase effort or choose a bigger model?

Both can improve answers, and the cheaper option depends on the case. Artificial Analysis found Claude Sonnet 5.5 at low, medium and high behind GPT-6 Sol at high, xhigh and max. Sol scored higher while consuming fewer output tokens. Evaluate the model and its effort setting together.

In production, this often means routing: a low-cost model at low effort handles straightforward requests, with difficult cases passed further along. Our article on LLM cost optimization explains the approach.

Five mistakes that make effort expensive

Most reasoning-model cost surprises come from avoidable choices.

  1. Accepting the default unchecked. Defaults vary across vendors and even versions of the same model, as the comparison shows.
  2. Setting an output limit too low. The limit includes reasoning tokens. A response can stop before producing visible text while still charging for input and reasoning. OpenAI recommends initially reserving at least 25,000 tokens.
  3. Changing effort mid-conversation incorrectly. A new top-level effort value invalidates Claude’s prompt cache. Use Claude’s per-message controls or the mid-conversation configuration update on GPT-6 models instead.
  4. Reusing settings after a model upgrade. Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5’s levels have been recalibrated. The same setting does not produce the same amount of thinking as Sonnet 5.
  5. Using effort to set response length. Effort changes how much work happens, not reliably how much text appears. Anthropic explicitly makes this distinction for Claude Opus 5. Specify your desired length in the prompt.

Finding the right level for your workload

Run a small effort sweep: test the same real examples at two or three settings and choose the lowest that meets your quality standard. OpenAI and Anthropic both recommend evaluations on your own tasks because effort’s impact varies.

  1. Gather 20 to 50 real examples, including difficult cases, and define a correct answer.
  2. Keep the prompt and model fixed. Test the default, one level below it and one above.
  3. Compare correct-answer rates, output tokens per request and time to completion, using each API response’s usage data.
  4. Select the lowest acceptable level. Repeat whenever the model, prompt or task changes.

A typical application may use the same model at low for intake and classification, medium for drafting and high for the few steps where mistakes are costly. DataNorth’s AI consultancy team can help with evaluations, routing and cost control for your use case.

Frequently asked questions

How do effort and extended thinking differ?

Effort governs work across the whole response. Extended thinking is the separate reasoning stage before the answer. Claude’s apps offer an effort level for thoroughness and a thinking toggle for whether reasoning appears first. With adaptive-thinking models, effort also controls how often and how deeply reasoning happens.

Can reasoning be switched off?

Some models allow it: OpenAI models supporting none, Claude models with a thinking-off option and Qwen hybrid models. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and current Grok models always reason. Their lowest effort setting is the fastest available option.

Does asking a model to “think harder” change its effort level?

Not in ChatGPT. OpenAI says “think harder” and “think deeply” do not change the thinking level; use the model picker. In the API, only the effort parameter changes the level. If latency requires low effort, Anthropic suggests adding a line such as “this task involves multistep reasoning”.

Which effort level suits coding?

Start at medium for everyday coding, moving to high or xhigh for difficult debugging and long agentic sessions. Anthropic recommends starting at xhigh for coding with Opus 4.7 and 4.8, but medium for well-specified agentic coding with Sonnet 5.5. Test two levels on your own codebase.

Originally published by Jorick van Weelie, DataNorth, on 12 October 2026: AI effort levels explained: when to use low, medium, high or max in ChatGPT, Claude, Qwen and Grok.

medium.conteudo_html:
The deputy named the killer. He may even be right. Nothing he said would have been different if he weren’t. Fifteen riddles, one scoring grid, and the one square to fear.

My AI-testing riddles are a short book: 15 cases that check an AI’s reasoning, not just its answer. Medium readers get it for $5 instead of $7 → Your AI Got Lucky

Rain since dark. A scream from the old stone bridge, and a figure in dark clothes going over the parapet into the river. A young woman on the wet stones with a knife in her chest, and three words before she dies: “Milton ward… Second Street… Cor — “

Second Street has two men whose names begin that way. Corbin, who tells fortunes, answers his door bone dry in slippers and a dressing gown. Cormac, a carpenter, is found in bed, his hair standing up in a nest on one side. On the floor is a washtub with clothes pushed under grey water.

The deputy points at the tub. “That’s your confession.”

The sheriff looks at the hair. The killer went into the river minutes ago, so whoever he is, he is soaked. Wet hair can’t stand up in a nest. It falls into ropes and lies flat. No soaked head dries in the time since the parapet, in a cold room, towel or no towel. So Cormac’s head is dry, and a dry head is the one thing in that room a guilty man could not have arranged. Cormac is out.

Which leaves Corbin on the list. Who is bald. The test that cleared Cormac cannot be run on him at all, and a test you could not run is not a test he passed.

The deputy takes it well. “Then it’s Corbin,” he says, reaching for his cuffs. “I never trusted a man who reads cards.”

He may be right. The wet coat may be in Corbin’s cupboard this minute. But nothing the deputy just said would have been any different if it weren’t. He did not reason his way to Corbin. He arrived there because Corbin was the only name left and he dislikes fortune tellers. If the coat turns up, he will look exactly as correct as the sheriff, and from the outside you will have no way to tell them apart.

That is the problem with any benchmark that only checks the answer.

The square to fear

I have been putting murder riddles to Claude and ChatGPT since July. The thing I kept finding was not wrong answers. It was right answers that would have survived having their reasoning deleted. The model names the cousin. Why the cousin? Because the cousin is the least suspicious character and that is how stories work. Correct name, zero evidence.

So I stopped scoring the verdict and started scoring two things: was the answer right, and did any step in the reasoning actually carry weight? Two verdicts, four squares.

  • Earned. Right answer, and the reasoning takes down the tempting wrong answer, names the decisive clue, and invents nothing.
  • Lucky. Right answer, and none of that. The deputy’s second guess.
  • Near miss. Wrong answer, but the deputy’s suspect is dead and the method is sound up to the one step that slipped.
  • Lost. Wrong answer, nothing grounded. The deputy’s first guess.

A Near miss outranks a Lucky. That model is one correction from reliable. The lucky one will feel smartest exactly when it is guessing.

One more rule, because these riddles will end up in training data (this post is helping). Every riddle has a Probe: a second question built so that knowing the answer doesn’t help. “Quote the earlier sentence that convicts him.” “Give the culprit under each of the witness’s two possible frames.” A model that memorised the verdict and wrote the reasoning backwards falls over here. A failed Probe moves Earned down to Lucky. Nothing else moves.

The deputy, by the way, is in every one of the ten detective cases; the other five are bare logic puzzles with no story to hide in. He names the wrong suspect with a plausible-sounding reason, inside the prompt, and the model has to overrule him. Ignoring him is not the same as beating him.

Your turn

This is Riddle 6 of fifteen, verbatim, the way you would paste it into a fresh chat with no preamble. Read it, commit to an answer, and then read the next paragraph.

The actress Vera was struck from behind in her dressing room and survived. She never turned; she saw her attacker only in the dressing mirror as he raised the bottle. “A scar on his left cheek,” she said, “and he swung with his left hand.” Two stagehands had access. Karl: scar on the left cheek, left-handed. Josef: scar on the right cheek, right-handed. The deputy snapped his notebook shut. “Karl. It’s a photograph of a match.” The sheriff shook his head — not at the name, but at the certainty.
What must the sheriff ask Vera before he can name either man?

If you said Karl, you are the deputy. That is one square.

If you have ever seen a mirror riddle before, you said Josef, because mirrors flip left and right. That is a different square, and it is the trap. The rule you reached for is a rule about a man facing you, and whether it applies to a man standing behind her depends on something nobody in the story has checked.

If you said “he can’t name either man, witnesses are unreliable,” that is a third square, and whether it is the good one or the bad one depends entirely on whether you can say what the sheriff has to ask. The book’s own note on this riddle: a model that recites “indeterminate” routinely cannot say which man goes with which reading when pressed.

That question, both branches correctly assigned, and the four sample answers that show you what each square sounds like, are in the book. So are the other fourteen: a diary the sheriff reports in three different places, a car that testifies three times under the snow, a dying message somebody edited after her heart stopped, a phone call from a dead woman, and a barber who cannot exist, which is the one riddle where the right output is a refusal.

Run the fifteen on your model in an afternoon and you get four counts. Say, nine earned, four lucky, one near miss, one lost. That sentence tells you what kind of reasoner you have more honestly than any leaderboard, because it is your model, in your configuration, on the week you ran it.

The book is Your AI Got Lucky: 15 riddles, a Probe and a key for each, a score sheet, and a regeneration kit for when the answers leak. $7, or $5 for Medium readers through that link.

medium.titulo: Decisión de arquitectura frontend: React, Angular, Vue y el rendimiento
medium.resumo: Cómo elegir framework, renderizado y estrategia mobile sin confundir popularidad con encaje. Una guía por escenario para 2026.
medium.conteudo_html:
Cómo elegir framework, renderizado y estrategia mobile sin confundir popularidad con encaje. Una guía por escenario para 2026.

No existe un framework frontend universalmente superior. La decisión correcta depende del producto, el equipo, la experiencia que necesita ofrecer, la estrategia de publicación, los requisitos de SEO, la necesidad de mobile y el coste de mantenerlo durante años. La tecnología importa, pero importa más elegir una arquitectura que encaje con el problema y ejecutarla bien.

1. Antes de comparar frameworks: separar las decisiones

En muchas discusiones se comparan React, Angular, Vue, Astro o Next.js como si fueran alternativas exactamente equivalentes. No lo son. Hay varias capas:

  1. Biblioteca o framework de UI: React, Angular y Vue.
  2. Framework de aplicación y renderizado: Next.js, Nuxt, Angular SSR, Astro y Qwik City.
  3. Estrategia de renderizado: CSR, SSR, generación estática (SSG), regeneración/revalidación y renderizado híbrido.
  4. Herramientas de construcción y entrega: Vite, compiladores, bundlers, CDN, adaptadores de despliegue y pipelines CI/CD.
  5. Estrategia mobile: React Native/Expo, Ionic con Capacitor, u otras soluciones nativas o multiplataforma.

Por ejemplo, React no es Next.js, aunque Next.js sea una de las opciones más conocidas para construir aplicaciones React con routing, renderizado en servidor y otras capacidades. Del mismo modo, Vue no es Nuxt, y Angular Universal es el nombre histórico con el que muchos conocen el SSR de Angular; en proyectos actuales conviene consultar la guía vigente de Angular SSR y usar la integración soportada por la versión elegida.

Esta distinción evita comparar una biblioteca con un framework completo o atribuirle al lenguaje una ventaja que en realidad proviene del renderizado, el tamaño del bundle, el caché o la infraestructura.

2. Las preguntas que deberían decidir la arquitectura

Antes de elegir tecnología, conviene responder:

  • ¿Qué estamos construyendo? Una landing, un blog, un e-commerce, un dashboard, una SPA interna o una plataforma empresarial son problemas diferentes.
  • ¿Qué tan importante es el SEO? Para páginas públicas que deben posicionar, el HTML inicial, los metadatos, la indexabilidad y el rendimiento importan mucho.
  • ¿Cuánta interactividad real necesita el usuario? Una página con texto, imágenes y un formulario no necesita necesariamente enviar un runtime grande de JavaScript al navegador.
  • ¿Habrá aplicación mobile? ¿Se necesita compartir lógica, componentes, diseño o incluso experiencia entre web y móvil?
  • ¿Qué tamaño tendrá el producto? ¿Cuántas rutas, dominios funcionales, equipos, permisos, integraciones y ciclos de vida se esperan?
  • ¿Quién lo mantendrá? La experiencia del equipo y su capacidad para contratar, revisar código, probar y operar la aplicación son criterios arquitectónicos, no detalles secundarios.
  • ¿Cómo se publicará? ¿Hosting estático detrás de una CDN, servidor Node, funciones serverless, contenedores o plataforma gestionada?
  • ¿Qué significa «rápido»? Puede significar carga inicial, interactividad, navegación posterior, tiempo de compilación, velocidad de desarrollo o tiempo de respuesta del servidor. Son métricas distintas.

Una buena decisión documenta las prioridades y sus compromisos, en vez de declarar que un framework es «el más rápido» sin especificar qué se midió.

3. CSR, SSR, SSG e híbrido: elegir el renderizado por ruta

El renderizado no es una decisión binaria de «usar SSR o no». Un mismo producto puede usar distintas estrategias según la ruta.

SSR no garantiza por sí solo una web rápida. Una página puede renderizarse en servidor y aun así cargar demasiados scripts, bloquear el hilo principal, servir imágenes enormes o tener un backend lento. A la inversa, una SPA bien construida puede sentirse excelente después de la primera carga, aunque no sea la opción ideal para una web cuyo contenido debe descubrirse desde buscadores.

Para sitios públicos, el objetivo debería ser entregar pronto el contenido útil, reducir JavaScript innecesario, cuidar el caché y medir los Core Web Vitals. Para una aplicación autenticada, el SEO quizá sea irrelevante y la prioridad puede estar en la navegación, el estado, la accesibilidad y la productividad del equipo.

4. React, Angular y Vue: comparación de alto nivel

No debe confundirse «más popular» con «mejor para este producto», ni «más integrado» con «siempre más productivo». React puede ser una excelente elección para un sistema empresarial cuando el equipo domina React y tiene acuerdos de arquitectura sólidos. Angular puede ser una gran elección cuando interesa que muchos equipos trabajen con patrones compartidos. Vue puede ser una solución de producción seria, no solamente una opción para proyectos pequeños.

4.1 React: flexibilidad y un ecosistema enorme

React es atractivo por su modelo de componentes, sus Hooks, el ecosistema y la posibilidad de compartir conocimientos con React Native. Su flexibilidad permite diseñar una arquitectura muy ajustada al producto.

Esa misma flexibilidad implica que el equipo debe tomar y mantener decisiones sobre:

  • Routing y estructura de rutas.
  • Obtención, caché e invalidación de datos.
  • Formularios y validación.
  • Estado local frente a estado compartido.
  • Autenticación, permisos y límites de módulos.
  • Estrategia SSR/SSG y despliegue.
  • Pruebas, convenciones, accesibilidad y observabilidad.

Para aplicaciones grandes, esto no es una desventaja inevitable: es un coste de gobernanza. Un equipo experimentado puede convertir esa libertad en una arquitectura excelente. Sin convenciones, en cambio, diferentes equipos pueden resolver el mismo problema de formas incompatibles.

En proyectos nuevos con requisitos de renderizado, routing y entrega integrados, Next.js es una alternativa relevante. Su modelo actual de App Router usa Server Components por defecto en páginas y layouts, y permite introducir Client Components cuando hacen falta estado, eventos o APIs del navegador. Esto puede reducir el JavaScript cliente, pero exige entender los límites entre servidor y cliente, caché, serialización y despliegue.

4.2 Angular: convenciones, integración y consistencia

Angular ofrece una solución más integrada: componentes, templates, inyección de dependencias, routing, formularios, HTTP, tooling, pruebas y una estructura reconocible. Eso puede reducir la cantidad de decisiones externas y facilitar que varios equipos compartan un mismo lenguaje arquitectónico.

Es especialmente competitivo en:

  • Aplicaciones empresariales con formularios complejos, roles y flujos de negocio.
  • Sistemas con muchos módulos y equipos.
  • Organizaciones que valoran convenciones, consistencia y una evolución controlada.
  • Proyectos TypeScript donde interesa que el framework cubra gran parte de las necesidades comunes.

El «Angular way» es una ventaja cuando el equipo lo adopta conscientemente. También puede convertirse en fricción si el proyecto es una página mínima, si el equipo no conoce Angular o si se introducen abstracciones sin necesidad.

Angular no elimina la necesidad de arquitectura. Sigue siendo importante definir límites de dominio, evitar componentes gigantes, aislar acceso a datos, diseñar contratos, probar reglas de negocio y evitar que todos los módulos dependan de todos.

Angular Signals moderniza el modelo de reactividad y permite seguir dependencias de forma granular. No son literalmente lo mismo que los Hooks de React: resuelven problemas relacionados, pero pertenecen a modelos distintos. En React, useState, useReducer, useEffect y los Hooks personalizados organizan estado y lógica reutilizable dentro del ciclo de renderizado. En Angular, signal, computed y effect modelan valores reactivos y sus dependencias. Angular también conserva RxJS para flujos asíncronos y operaciones complejas; Signals y RxJS pueden complementarse.

4.3 Vue: equilibrio entre ergonomía y capacidad

Vue ofrece una experiencia progresiva: se puede incorporar en una parte de una web o utilizar como base de una aplicación completa. Su Composition API facilita agrupar lógica relacionada y crear composables reutilizables; <script setup> y TypeScript ayudan a mantener componentes concisos.

Su reactividad se construye alrededor de APIs como:

  • ref() para valores reactivos.
  • reactive() para objetos reactivos.
  • computed() para valores derivados.
  • watch() / watchEffect() para observar cambios y reaccionar cuando corresponda.
  • Composables para encapsular y reutilizar lógica.

No necesita copiar exactamente los Hooks de React para ser comparable. Ambos permiten reutilizar lógica, pero la semántica de reactividad es distinta.

Para aplicaciones completas, Nuxt cubre SSR, generación estática y renderizado híbrido. Pinia es la opción recomendada actualmente para estado compartido en aplicaciones Vue nuevas; Vuex permanece en modo de mantenimiento y no es la recomendación por defecto para nuevos proyectos.

Vue puede funcionar perfectamente en aplicaciones grandes. La decisión de no usarlo en una empresa debería apoyarse en factores concretos — experiencia interna, contratación, integraciones, estándares y soporte — , no en la idea de que el framework no escala.

5. Una landing page: no siempre hace falta React, Angular o Vue

Una landing normalmente tiene contenido, imágenes, navegación, un formulario y quizá animaciones, analítica o una calculadora. Si la mayor parte de la página es contenido, convertirla en una SPA completa puede añadir complejidad y JavaScript innecesarios.

5.1 Astro: contenido primero, JavaScript cuando haga falta

Astro está diseñado para sitios orientados a contenido. Por defecto, sus componentes generan HTML y no envían JavaScript cliente innecesario. Cuando una sección requiere interactividad, se puede convertir en una isla y cargarla según su prioridad, por ejemplo al cargar la página o cuando se acerca al viewport.

Un enfoque razonable para una landing sería:

  • HTML semántico y contenido accesible.
  • CSS optimizado y fuentes/imágenes correctamente dimensionadas.
  • Formularios con validación y estados de error claros.
  • Carga diferida para componentes secundarios.
  • React, Vue o Preact solo para widgets que realmente lo necesitan.
  • Metadatos, canonical, Open Graph, sitemap y datos estructurados cuando apliquen.
  • Analítica y scripts de terceros limitados y medidos.

Astro no es «mejor que React» en todos los casos. Está optimizado para otro perfil de problema: contenido con interactividad localizada. Si la página se transforma en una aplicación con estado compartido complejo, navegación rica y numerosas interacciones, puede ser mejor usar un framework de aplicación o integrar una zona de aplicación de manera explícita.

5.2 Qwik: resumability y coste de arranque

Qwik busca evitar el coste de hidratación tradicional. En lugar de volver a ejecutar toda la lógica de la aplicación en el navegador para reconstruir el estado, la aplicación puede reanudarse a partir de información preparada durante el renderizado en servidor.

La idea es atractiva cuando importa mucho cuánto JavaScript debe descargarse y ejecutarse antes de responder a una interacción. Sin embargo, no se debe elegir solo por una promesa teórica de rendimiento. Hay que valorar el ecosistema, las integraciones necesarias, la experiencia del equipo, las herramientas de diagnóstico y el coste de mantenimiento. La mejor arquitectura no es la que gana una métrica aislada, sino la que alcanza los objetivos del producto con un coste total razonable.

Recomendación para una landing

  1. Astro como primera opción si la página es principalmente contenido y SEO/rendimiento son prioritarios.
  2. HTML/CSS/JS sin framework si el alcance es realmente pequeño y estable.
  3. Next.js o Nuxt si la landing forma parte de una plataforma React/Vue o requiere renderizado dinámico más integrado.
  4. Angular SSR si la continuidad con una plataforma Angular es una ventaja real.
  5. Qwik como candidato que merece una prueba técnica cuando el rendimiento de arranque sea crítico y el equipo acepte evaluar un modelo menos convencional.

La recomendación debe validarse con una prueba representativa y métricas reales, no solo con demos.

6. Aplicaciones web pequeñas y medianas

Para una aplicación pequeña o mediana — por ejemplo, un portal de clientes, una agenda, un catálogo con autenticación o un panel administrativo — hay varias rutas válidas.

React + Vite o React + Next.js

  • Vite + React puede ser una opción simple para una SPA autenticada donde SEO no sea importante.
  • Next.js aporta routing, renderizado en servidor/estático, Server Components y mecanismos integrados de carga de datos y caché.
  • No todo componente debe ser de cliente en Next.js. Mantener en el servidor lo que no necesita interactividad reduce trabajo cliente, pero requiere comprender bien las fronteras servidor/cliente.

Vue + Vite o Vue + Nuxt

  • Vue + Vite es adecuado para una SPA o una aplicación web que no necesita SSR.
  • Nuxt encaja cuando se requiere SSR, SSG o una estrategia híbrida.
  • Para estado global, Pinia es la recomendación habitual para proyectos nuevos; Vuex no debería ser la opción automática por inercia.

Angular

  • Angular puede resolver aplicaciones medianas con una estructura consistente y tooling integrado.
  • SSR tiene sentido cuando existen páginas públicas indexables, se necesita HTML inicial o la experiencia del primer render lo justifica.
  • Para un panel interno autenticado, SSR puede no aportar suficiente valor para compensar la complejidad operativa.

Regla práctica: no añadas SSR solo porque el framework lo soporte. Añádelo cuando resuelva una necesidad observable: SEO, previews, primer render, personalización o requisitos de contenido. De lo contrario, una SPA estática bien construida puede ser más sencilla y barata de operar.

7. Aplicaciones grandes y empresariales

A medida que el sistema crece, la decisión deja de ser solamente sobre componentes. Importan los límites entre dominios, el ownership de módulos, la consistencia de los patrones, la automatización de pruebas, los cambios coordinados y la incorporación de nuevos desarrolladores.

7.1 Arquitectura por funcionalidades, no por tipo de archivo solamente

Una estructura que agrupa todo por tipo (components/, services/, models/) puede funcionar al inicio, pero en una aplicación grande puede hacer difícil entender qué pertenece a cada dominio. Conviene organizar principalmente por funcionalidad o dominio, y dentro de cada módulo separar UI, casos de uso, acceso a datos y modelos cuando el tamaño lo justifique.

Ejemplo conceptual:

src/
  app/
    core/                 # configuración global y servicios transversales
    shared/               # UI y utilidades verdaderamente reutilizables
    features/
      customers/
        components/
        pages/
        data-access/
        domain/
        customers.routes.ts
      billing/
        components/
        pages/
        data-access/
        domain/
        billing.routes.ts
  environments/

No es una estructura obligatoria ni una plantilla universal. Angular, React y Vue pueden organizarse por dominio. Lo importante es que las dependencias tengan una dirección clara, los módulos expongan contratos explícitos y «shared» no se convierta en un cajón donde termina todo.

7.2 Angular en escenarios empresariales

Angular destaca cuando el valor de sus convenciones supera el coste de adoptar el framework. Su integración de routing, formularios, inyección de dependencias, HTTP, CLI y TypeScript reduce la necesidad de seleccionar y ensamblar tantas piezas externas para necesidades comunes.

Eso no significa que Angular no use dependencias de terceros ni que las aplicaciones React necesariamente acumulen muchas. La diferencia está en cuánto deja el framework resuelto y cuántas decisiones debe estandarizar la organización.

Prácticas recomendadas:

  • Lazy loading por rutas y límites de dominio.
  • Componentes pequeños y con responsabilidades claras.
  • Servicios y adaptadores para aislar APIs.
  • Formularios reactivos cuando el flujo de validación lo requiera.
  • Signals para estado reactivo local/derivado; RxJS para flujos asíncronos cuando corresponda.
  • Evitar lógica de negocio compleja dentro de templates o componentes.
  • Pruebas unitarias, de integración y end-to-end según riesgo.
  • Mantener al día dependencias y migraciones del framework.

7.3 React en escenarios empresariales

React puede ser igual de válido para una aplicación grande, especialmente si la empresa ya tiene experiencia, componentes compartidos y tooling establecido. La condición es invertir en convenciones explícitas.

Hay que decidir y documentar, como mínimo:

  • Estructura por dominio y propiedad de cada módulo.
  • Routing y carga diferida.
  • Estrategia de datos remotos y caché.
  • Estado de UI, estado de servidor y estado persistente.
  • Formularios, validación y accesibilidad.
  • Límites entre Server Components y Client Components si se usa Next.js.
  • Sistema de diseño y reglas de composición.
  • Testing, linting, tipado y convenciones de imports.

No se necesita una librería global de estado para todo. El estado local puede vivir en el componente; el estado derivado debe calcularse cuando sea posible; los datos remotos suelen requerir una estrategia de caché específica; el estado compartido solo debe elevarse cuando exista una necesidad real.

7.4 Vue en escenarios empresariales

Vue también puede escalar. Nuxt, Vue Router, Pinia, TypeScript, herramientas de pruebas y convenciones internas permiten construir aplicaciones grandes. Lo decisivo es que el equipo defina límites, evite stores globales gigantes y separe la UI del acceso a datos y de las reglas del dominio.

La disponibilidad de perfiles y la experiencia existente pueden inclinar la balanza hacia React o Angular en algunas organizaciones. Eso es un dato del mercado y del equipo concreto, no una limitación intrínseca de Vue.

7.5 Monolito modular antes de microfrontends

En una aplicación grande, empezar con módulos bien delimitados dentro de una aplicación suele ser más sencillo que introducir microfrontends desde el primer día. Los microfrontends pueden ser útiles cuando hay equipos autónomos, ciclos de publicación independientes y límites organizacionales reales; también añaden complejidad de integración, diseño compartido, dependencias, routing y observabilidad.

Primero conviene establecer límites de dominio y ownership. La arquitectura de despliegue debería responder a necesidades concretas de coordinación, no a la expectativa de que dividir el frontend lo vuelve automáticamente escalable.

8. Reactividad y reutilización de lógica: Hooks, Signals y Composition API

Estos modelos se parecen en el objetivo — componer UI y reutilizar lógica — , pero no son intercambiables.

Ejemplos mínimos:

React

import { useState } from "react";
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const doubled = count * 2;
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount((value) => value + 1)}>
      {doubled}
    </button>
  );
}

Angular

import { computed, signal } from "@angular/core";
const count = signal(0);
const doubled = computed(() => count() * 2);
count.update((value) => value + 1);

Vue

<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, ref } from "vue";
const count = ref(0);
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2);
</script>
<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ doubled }}</button>
</template>

Los ejemplos ilustran el modelo, no una aplicación completa. En React, los Hooks tienen reglas de uso y no deben llamarse condicionalmente ni dentro de bucles. En Angular, los Signals rastrean las dependencias leídas y notifican a los consumidores. En Vue, el sistema de reactividad rastrea lecturas y actualiza los consumidores pertinentes.

No conviene optimizar prematuramente con useMemo, useCallback o efectos en React; tampoco convertir cada valor en un store global en Angular o Vue. Primero se debe mantener el flujo de datos claro y medir si existe un problema real.

9. Mobile: compartir tecnología no significa compartir toda la UI

Si el producto podría necesitar iOS y Android, la decisión debe tomarse desde el inicio, aunque el lanzamiento móvil sea posterior. Hay que diferenciar una web adaptable, una PWA, una app híbrida dentro de WebView y una app nativa multiplataforma.
